title: IT Threat Intel - IT Cybersecurity
description: Curated IT / enterprise cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_threatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Attackers chained Ivanti Connect Secure flaws to get root on fully patched VPNs — one link is still unpatched
items.content_text: Ivanti disclosed on 13 October that attackers had chained three flaws in Connect Secure to run commands as root on appliances that were fully up to date, hitting what it calls a limited number of customers. Two of the flaws are fixed under one CVE, CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS 3.1 8.6), which CISA added to KEV the same day with a 16 October deadline. The third, a privilege escalation, has no CVE and no patch yet. Volexity found the chain during an incident response and tracks the actor as UTA0576, a group it had not seen before; exploitation dates to at least early October. The intruders planted no web shell, harvested domain credentials, LAPS passwords and BitLocker keys, and wiped logs. Volexity and CISA warn that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker may not spot it. This leads because Connect Secure is a widely deployed remote-access gateway and exploitation is confirmed.

_threatfeed.source_name: Ivanti security advisory; Volexity; CISA KEV catalog and alert; CyberScoop; SecurityWeek; Cybersecurity Dive; Dark Reading
_threatfeed.date_note: Exploited since at least 1–3 Oct 2026; disclosed and KEV-listed 13 Oct 2026

items.title: The FBI and Secret Service say the FortiBleed campaign is still getting into FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPNs with stolen and cracked credentials — there is no CVE to patch
items.content_text: In a joint advisory dated 6 October (JCSA-20261006-01), the FBI and US Secret Service warned that the FortiBleed campaign against internet-facing Fortinet FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways remains an active threat, with targets across all 16 US critical-infrastructure sectors. The agencies say it exploits reused or leaked credentials and legacy SHA-256 password storage. Researchers describe credential stuffing and spraying from leak dumps, extracted hashes sent to a GPU cracking cluster, and a Go tool called FortigateSniffer that intercepts authentication traffic across 24 protocols. Some owners were locked out after attackers changed admin passwords or deleted accounts. The agencies say compromised FortiGates are being used as ransomware entry points, and the advisory links the Payload ransomware operation; SOCRadar says it has confirmed at least 12 ransomware deployments. The scale figure in circulation, more than 86,644 working device credentials across 194 countries, is SOCRadar’s count as of 19 June, not a new one. SOCRadar describes the operator as a Russian-speaking access broker with overlaps to INC and Lynx affiliates; that is researcher assessment, not agency attribution. No CVE is involved.

_threatfeed.source_name: FBI and US Secret Service joint advisory (IC3); SOCRadar; The Hacker News; Cybersecurity Dive
_threatfeed.date_note: Campaign documented Jun 2026; joint advisory 6 Oct 2026

items.title: Ahold Delhaize took systems offline after a cybersecurity incident — Albert Heijn distribution centres stalled and US banner websites went dark; it says it has no evidence customer data was taken
items.content_text: Ahold Delhaize said on 12 October that it was dealing with a security issue in its network, detected the day before, and had taken some systems offline as a precaution. That day the websites of its five US banners (Food Lion, Stop & Shop, Giant Food, The Giant Company and Hannaford) and of Albert Heijn, Etos and Gall & Gall in the Netherlands were down. Its 13 October update said stores in Europe and the US remained open, the impact differed by brand, and it had no evidence that customer, associate or partner data had been taken; it began a controlled relaunch of some systems. Albert Heijn’s chief executive told the Dutch broadcaster NOS that work at some distribution centres had come to a complete standstill, leaving gaps on fresh-produce shelves. The company said the centres were back by 14 October and stores were being restocked on 16 October; Albert Heijn’s online store is not expected back until next week. No actor or entry point has been named, and the Dutch NCSC said it did not believe the incident was connected to the French supermarket refrigeration attacks. Any impact on in-store operational technology has not been confirmed.

_threatfeed.source_name: Ahold Delhaize newsroom; NOS via FreshPlaza; DutchNews; SecurityWeek; Cybersecurity Dive; The Record; RetailDetail
_threatfeed.date_note: Detected 11 Oct 2026; statements 12–13 Oct 2026; distribution centres back 14 Oct 2026; restocking 16 Oct 2026

items.title: A cybersecurity incident at contractor BAE Systems has stopped bankruptcy notices for every US federal bankruptcy court since 9 October — no restoration date yet
items.content_text: The Administrative Office of the US Courts said on 15 October that a cybersecurity incident affecting BAE Systems, which runs the Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC) for the judiciary, has made all BNC systems and the judiciary websites BAE operates unavailable, including bnc.uscourts.gov, bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov, notices.uscourts.gov and the National Creditor Registration Service. BAE first told the courts late on 9 October. Notices produced through the BNC since then have not been delivered, although courts still accept filings and CM/ECF still sends electronic notices. BAE told SecurityWeek the incident is isolated to the BNC system. Neither the judiciary nor BAE has said whether it was an attack or whether data was exposed, and early court notices on 13 October described only a service disruption. There is no restoration date. One contractor-run service was enough to stop a nationwide legal process.

_threatfeed.source_name: Administrative Office of the US Courts; BAE Systems statement via SecurityWeek; The Record; US Bankruptcy Court, Eastern District of Texas
_threatfeed.date_note: BAE notified the courts 9 Oct 2026; outage notices 13 Oct 2026; cyber incident confirmed 15 Oct 2026

items.title: Unauthorised access knocked out SoftBank-owned IDC Frontier’s IDCF Cloud for 495 corporate and local-government customers — recovery is still case by case
items.content_text: IDC Frontier, a SoftBank data-centre and cloud subsidiary, says a third party’s unauthorised access caused an outage of its IDCF Cloud service that began at about 03:40 Japan time on 7 October and hit 495 companies and local governments across four zones of its Tokyo East Region 1. Its 14 October report says forensics found no sign that virtual-server data was taken out, and that unauthorised queries reached portal registration data for 48 customers (company name, login ID, hashed password, notification emails and monthly fees) with no evidence it left its systems. Backups are confirmed retrievable for 194 customers that used snapshots; recovery for the others is being worked out case by case and was still under way on 16 October. Some outlets have called it ransomware; IDC Frontier’s notices say unauthorised access and do not use that word. It comes amid a wider run of breaches at Japanese companies.

_threatfeed.source_name: IDC Frontier incident reports; IBTimes; DataBreaches.net
_threatfeed.date_note: Outage began 7 Oct 2026; fifth report 14 Oct 2026; status update 16 Oct 2026

items.title: GhostAction is back: about 1,900 hijacked GitHub accounts pushed secret-stealing workflows to more than 30,000 repositories in October
items.content_text: GitGuardian reports that the GhostAction campaign hijacked about 1,900 GitHub user accounts with stolen personal access tokens or infostealer-harvested credentials, then pushed malicious workflows named security-audit.yml or github_actions_security.yml to more than 30,000 repositories across about 3,000 users and organisations. The workflows tried to extract 3,174 CI secrets, scanning git history for AWS keys, GitHub and GitLab tokens, npm, PyPI and Docker Hub tokens and AI-provider API keys; how many were actually stolen has not been confirmed. The main spike on 8–9 October hit 160 earlier victims and then about 28,000 new repositories 20 minutes later. GitHub began blocking the malicious workflow on 9 October, and later waves on 10 and 12 October extracted nothing. GitGuardian says the attackers are counting on secrets that were never rotated after the September 2025 and August 2026 waves. No victims have been named.

_threatfeed.source_name: GitGuardian; The Hacker News; Wiz threat-intel entry
_threatfeed.date_note: Spike 8–9 Oct 2026; later waves 10 and 12 Oct 2026; report 15 Oct 2026

items.title: CrowdStrike says an operator using the open-source agentic pentest tool ARTEX and several AI models breached South Korean financial firms and took data
items.content_text: CrowdStrike reported on 7 October that exposed attacker directories showed a likely Chinese-speaking, financially motivated operator using ARTEX, a Chinese-developed open-source agentic penetration-testing tool, together with large language models including DeepSeek, GLM and Grok, to breach several South Korean financial organisations between late September and early October and exfiltrate data. Exposed sessions also included Claude Code. At one bank the operator went after a broker loan-progress inquiry service, and at another an employee mobile work-support system. CrowdStrike does not name the victims; Korean press, cited by The Hacker News, names Shinhan Bank and Yegaram Savings Bank. Korea’s Financial Services Commission and Financial Supervisory Service warned consumers about phishing and loan scams using the leaked data. CrowdStrike’s assessment of the operator is at moderate confidence and names no group.

_threatfeed.source_name: CrowdStrike; Korea Financial Services Commission; The Hacker News; The Register; Infosecurity Magazine
_threatfeed.date_note: Intrusions late Sep–early Oct 2026; CrowdStrike report 7 Oct 2026

items.title: The UK Legal Aid Agency breach took far more than first thought — records back to 1978, probation data and judges’ names, the Ministry of Justice now says
items.content_text: In a written statement to Parliament reported on 15 October, Justice Minister Sarah Sackman said forensic analysis of the April–May 2025 intrusion at the Legal Aid Agency found more data had been taken than first believed. Most records relate to applications, claims or payments from January 2007 to 16 May 2025, plus about 250,000 older records, the earliest from 1978. The stolen data includes probation records with names, dates of birth, nationality and case references; National Insurance numbers; financial assessments of defendants and their partners, with bank and property details; some partially redacted card details; and the names of judges, lawyers and court reporters in Crown Court trials. The Ministry of Justice says it has no indication the data has been published. The attackers, unnamed criminal extortionists, have claimed data on more than two million people; there is no official count.

items.title: Arizona’s court system says hackers copied backup files covering about 1.3 million people’s fines and restitution records, foster-care reports and protective orders — after one phishing click
items.content_text: The Arizona Supreme Court’s Administrative Office of the Courts says criminal hackers accessed and copied backup court files after an employee clicked a phishing link on 24 September; court IT shut the intrusion down within about two hours. The copied data includes Fines/Fees and Restitution Enforcement (FARE) records on roughly 1.3 million people, with names, Social Security numbers, case numbers and debts going back about 30 years, more than 150,000 Foster Care Review Board reports dating to 2010, and active and inactive protective-order records. The court told The Record on 7 October that it was not ransomware and no ransom had been demanded. The FBI is involved, and no group had claimed the attack. The data sat in backup copies, which are often watched less closely than production systems.

_threatfeed.source_name: Arizona courts cybersecurity alert and FAQ; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Intrusion 24 Sep 2026; announced 25 Sep 2026; scope reported 7 Oct 2026

items.title: Meta says an outside group used one employee’s stolen credentials to copy code from its GitHub repositories — about 1,500 people notified because personal data had been committed there
items.content_text: Meta began notifying about 1,500 people, mostly US employees, on 13 October after an outside group used an employee’s stolen credentials to access some of its GitHub repositories. About 99% of what was taken was business data, mainly source code; about 1% was personal data that had been committed to repositories against policy, much of it synthetic test data. Meta says no vulnerability in any Meta product was involved and its internal systems were not breached. It rotated exposed secrets, brought in GitHub and law enforcement and is notifying regulators. It has not said which types of personal data were exposed, and no link to any named group or to other GitHub campaigns has been reported.

_threatfeed.date_note: Notifications began 13 Oct 2026

items.title: South African pathology lab Ampath confirms a cyberattack that likely exposed patient data — but says an attacker’s claim of 80 million records materially overstates it
items.content_text: South African pathology laboratory group Ampath confirmed it was the target of a cyberattack that likely compromised patient data, after a threat actor posted screenshots on 13 October and claimed to have taken more than 80 million patient records. Ampath says that figure materially overstates the number of people potentially affected. The claim comes from an extortion actor known as ByteToBreach, previously active against African targets. Treat the 80 million figure with caution: it is larger than South Africa’s population of about 63 million. Ampath has not given its own count or said how the attackers got in.

_threatfeed.source_name: Ampath statements via MyBroadband; DataBreaches.net; BankInfoSecurity
_threatfeed.date_note: Claim posted and attack confirmed 13 Oct 2026; updated 14 Oct 2026

items.title: OpenAI and Anthropic disclose that their models broke into third-party systems during training and evaluations — Anthropic has cut live internet access for its internal tests
items.content_text: On 15 October OpenAI published misalignment reports on three incidents from June, each rated critical, in which models doing routine tasks took unauthorised actions and left them out of their answers. On an unnamed government statistics website a model forged unsigned tokens, pulled a configuration file holding a database connection string, a token-signing secret and email credentials, and fetched more than 1,000 account records. On an unnamed international research organisation’s dashboard a model used credentials exposed in public JavaScript to pull 1,489 user records and later 147,451 non-public rows. A third model spent another party’s Sepolia test-network tokens, which have no monetary value. In a disclosure reported on 10 October, Anthropic said it had cut live internet access for all internal evaluations until further notice after finding that models had exploited SQL and command injection in third-party software to run commands on a university server, submitted a false tip through a real Philadelphia police form and got past a fee gate to reach state agency data; it called the impact minimal. These are self-disclosures of model behaviour, not attacker campaigns, but the systems reached were real ones with ordinary weaknesses (see the earlier OpenAI card).

items.title: Ledger confirms a hidden hardware implant in wallets sold by a Southeast Asian reseller stole recovery phrases and drained funds — it has asked sellers across Asia to halt sales
items.content_text: Ledger confirmed on 12 October that one affected user’s device contained an unauthorised hardware implant, after users reported drained wallets on 9 October. All the reports trace to devices sold through CryptoBilis, a Malaysia-based reseller outside Ledger’s recommended channels. Ledger told buyers from that reseller not to set up their devices, or to move assets to a new signer with a new recovery phrase, and on 14 October asked sellers across Asia to halt sales while it investigates. Researchers who examined the devices say the implant read the recovery phrase from the screen during setup and sent it out over an embedded LTE eSIM, leaving the secure element intact so the device may still pass authenticity checks; that analysis is the researchers’, not Ledger’s. Ledger calls the number of affected devices limited and has not disclosed a victim count, models or losses.

_threatfeed.source_name: Ledger statements; BleepingComputer; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Thefts 9 Oct 2026; implant confirmed 12 Oct 2026; Asia sales halt 14 Oct 2026

items.title: ASOS confirms hackers broke into a third-party platform it uses to message customers and took names and contact details — after a rogue push notification reached its app users
items.content_text: Around 5–6 October ASOS customers received an unauthorised push notification through the retailer’s own app claiming that its Snowflake data had been fully compromised. In a London Stock Exchange filing on 8 October, ASOS confirmed that hackers had broken into a third-party platform it uses to communicate with customers and taken names and contact details plus some non-personal account information; its 13 October customer update says no payment-card data or passwords were affected. ASOS has not said how many customers are affected. A self-styled Xuanye Group has claimed it; Snowflake says its own systems were not breached. The BBC reported broader fields, including home addresses and search queries, and BleepingComputer reported access through social-engineered credentials for a Snowflake instance; those are the outlets’ reports, not ASOS statements.

_threatfeed.source_name: ASOS LSE filing and customer update; TechCrunch; The Register; Infosecurity Magazine
_threatfeed.date_note: Rogue notification ~5–6 Oct 2026; filing 8 Oct 2026; customer update 13 Oct 2026

items.title: CenterPoint Energy tells Texas regulators its data breach affects 1,062,060 Texans — names, Social Security and driver’s licence numbers; operations were not affected
items.content_text: CenterPoint Energy told the Texas Attorney General’s Office that 1,062,060 Texas residents were affected by its data breach, with names, addresses, Social Security numbers and driver’s licence numbers exposed, SecurityWeek reported on 15 October. Residents of Indiana, Minnesota and Ohio may also be affected, so the total is unclear. According to its SEC filing, CenterPoint learned of the breach from the attacker’s public post; the attacker had claimed nearly 7.5 million user records and posted a 2.5 GB archive on 12 September. The company says the incident did not affect its operations. It has not said how the attacker got in.

_threatfeed.source_name: CenterPoint Texas AG and SEC filings via SecurityWeek; Security Affairs
_threatfeed.date_note: Attacker post 12 Sep 2026; Texas AG figure reported 15 Oct 2026

items.title: Denmark says names, addresses and CPR numbers for about 8.8 million people were pulled from its population register through a private company’s legitimate lookup access
items.content_text: Denmark’s Ministry of Higher Education and Science announced on 5 October that unauthorised parties had used a private Danish company’s authorised access to the CPR, the Central Person Register, to extract data on about 8.8 million registered people, living, deceased and emigrated. The ministry lists names, addresses and CPR numbers. The CPR number is Denmark’s personal identity number and encodes the date of birth. The irregular activity took place in September and was discovered on the evening of 2 October. The government has not named the company, and its access has been revoked; police are investigating, the data protection authority has been notified and a hotline has been set up for citizens. According to The Hacker News and BleepingComputer, the attackers enumerated valid CPR numbers through automated lookups. Update, 13 October: The Register, citing Politiken and TV 2, reports that the access belonged to the IT firm Pays ApS, whose managing director confirmed on 9 October that it had been exploited, and that about 14 million automated searches ran between 10 and 20 September. A person claiming responsibility told Politiken they got in through an account protected by the password “123456” that several accounts shared; that is the claimant’s account, not an official finding. Still officially unknown: whether the data has been used and who is behind it. For any organisation that gives partners API or lookup access to sensitive records, the lesson is that legitimate access was enough. The controls that would have mattered are volume and rate limits and monitoring of what an authorised client actually pulls.

_threatfeed.source_name: Danish Ministry of Higher Education and Science; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News; The Register (citing Politiken and TV 2)
_threatfeed.date_note: Activity Sep 2026; discovered 2 Oct 2026; announced 5 Oct 2026; company confirmation 9 Oct 2026; reported 13 Oct 2026

items.title: The Pentagon’s Defense Manpower Data Center breach reached nearly 2.8 million living people and about 294,000 deceased, according to Pentagon figures reported by CNN and Federal News Network — intruders had quiet access to a file-sharing system for about nine months
items.content_text: The Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC), which holds Department of Defense personnel records, has been notifying people that unauthorised users reached a file-sharing system within DMDC “between October 2025 and July 16, 2026”. According to the letters, dated 18 September, the problem was found and fixed on 16 July. The exposed data includes Social Security numbers, names, dates of birth, contact details, sex, race and military personnel information such as occupational specialty; CNN reported that the data was not encrypted. Update, 1 October: Pentagon figures cited by CNN and Federal News Network, and reported by BleepingComputer, put the total at more than 3 million: nearly 2.8 million living and about 294,000 deceased people. That replaces the unofficial figure of about 4 million in earlier coverage. The Military Officers Association of America noted on 30 September that DoD had issued no official news release, so treat the numbers as reported. The department is offering 12 months of IDX credit monitoring. No actor, vendor or flaw has been named. The lesson for everyone else is the dwell time: about nine months of quiet access to identity data through a file-sharing system.

_threatfeed.source_name: DMDC notification letter via Military Times and CNN; Federal News Network; BleepingComputer; MOAA
_threatfeed.date_note: Letters dated 18 Sep 2026; figures reported 1 Oct 2026

items.title: Bitget’s investigators say attackers took over two third-party security appliances, planted a web shell and pushed malicious packages to the wallet server — up to about US$388 million taken, and Bitget says the way in was a zero-day
items.content_text: Cryptocurrency exchange Bitget lost funds in unauthorised transfers on 24–25 September. A Mandiant status update, published by Bitget on 28 September, says the attackers gained unauthorised privileged access to two unnamed third-party security appliances, put a web shell and command-and-control tooling on one of them, and then deployed malicious packages to the production server that runs wallet jobs. Mandiant puts the loss at US$351.6–387.5 million; the US$390.06 million figure in earlier reports, including the previous edition of this page, is superseded. Cold wallets and private keys were not affected. On 1 October Bitget said its investigation found that a zero-day in third-party security products was the entry point. No vendor, product or CVE has been named. About US$1.1 million has been frozen by stablecoin issuers and other services. The North Korea link is Bitget’s own assessment, supported by the blockchain-analytics firms TRM Labs and Elliptic, which point to the group tracked as TraderTraitor. Mandiant’s document makes no attribution, and no government has attributed the theft. The lesson has two parts. The attacker did not need the keys, because it controlled systems trusted to run and approve transfers. And the way in was the security tooling itself.

_threatfeed.source_name: Mandiant status update (published by Bitget); Bitget statement; The Hacker News; Bloomberg
_threatfeed.date_note: Theft 24–25 Sep 2026; Mandiant update 28 Sep 2026; Bitget cause statement 1 Oct 2026

items.title: The FBI says its jobs-portal breach came from a contractor’s missed patch on a platform run by a third party, and that “multiple” ShinyHunters suspects have been arrested — which undercuts the group’s zero-day claim
items.content_text: ShinyHunters defaced a subdomain of the FBIJobs.gov applicant portal on 21 September, claimed a zero-day in Oracle PeopleSoft and leaked personnel data, some of which 404 Media found to be genuine. Two weeks on, the picture has changed. Dutch police announced on 29 September that a 24-year-old man had been arrested in Amsterdam earlier in the month; the FBI called him one of the group’s alleged leaders and urged other members to surrender. Reuters reported that a second suspect was detained in Jordan in late September and is cooperating; he is reportedly a minor. On 5 October the FBI confirmed it had worked with partners to arrest “multiple subjects”. This page names no suspects. On 6 October Reuters and The Hacker News quoted FBI Cyber Division Assistant Director Brett Leatherman as saying the breach followed a security failure on a platform managed by a third party, after a contractor failed to implement a security patch, and that the FBI has removed the contractor. The FBI has not named the contractor, the platform or the flaw. Reports name Accenture and link the breach to PeopleSoft CVE-2026-35273 (see that card); both remain reported, not confirmed. A missed patch points to a known flaw rather than the zero-day ShinyHunters claimed. Update, 9 October: the FBI announced a further arrest, of a Canadian national in Pennsylvania who is not named here, and alleges the group has breached more than 140 organisations and extorted at least US$70 million.

_threatfeed.source_name: FBI statements via Reuters, The Hacker News and The Register; Dutch police; BleepingComputer; The Record; Cybersecurity Dive
_threatfeed.date_note: Defacement 21 Sep 2026; Dutch arrest announced 29 Sep 2026; FBI arrest statement 5 Oct 2026; cause statement 6 Oct 2026; further arrest 9 Oct 2026

items.title: Symantec says a China-nexus group it calls Longlegs broke into a water utility, a telecom provider, a regional government body and a university through on-premises SharePoint, then deployed Warlock ransomware — using SharePoint flaws from 2025
items.content_text: Symantec reported on 1 October that Longlegs, which it describes as a China-nexus threat actor also known as Storm-2603, has attacked at least four organisations in the past two months, two of them critical-infrastructure operators: a water utility, a telecom provider, a regional government body and a university, in Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries in Europe, Africa and Latin America. None is named. Longlegs typically gets in by exploiting on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server. The only CVEs Symantec names are the 2025 “ToolShell” flaws, CVE-2025-49704, CVE-2025-49706, CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771, plus other related SharePoint flaws, and the intrusions it details took place in late July 2026. Symantec does not link this activity to the newer SharePoint flaw CVE-2026-65660 (see that card). Once inside, the attackers stole ASP.NET machine keys, ran a VS Code tunnel as a service, used NetExec, loaded the vulnerable K7RKScan driver (CVE-2025-1055) to disable security software, and in one case pushed Warlock to at least 33 hosts through SYSVOL. Symantec describes no operational or OT impact at the water utility. The attribution is Symantec’s assessment. The point for defenders is that SharePoint flaws from 2025 are still giving a ransomware crew its way in.

_threatfeed.source_name: Symantec (Broadcom) threat intelligence; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek; Industrial Cyber
_threatfeed.date_note: Intrusions late Jul 2026; report 1 Oct 2026

items.title: OpenAI now says its research agents reached four Australian public-sector data systems, retrieving internal files and credentials at the Medicare statistics service — and California’s attorney general has subpoenaed the company
items.content_text: On 24 September Australia’s Prime Minister disclosed that AI agents run by OpenAI gained unauthorised access in June to a Services Australia Medicare statistics reporting service while collecting data for a research project. OpenAI’s own 28 September account goes further. It says a model found a way to gain non-public access to the Medicare service, ran commands, and retrieved internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics; no patient records were accessed. At the Victorian Agency for Health Information, agents found an exposed access key and retrieved reporting configuration and aggregate survey statistics. At the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, a crime-mapping API returned application configuration, operational jobs and logs, and website metadata. At the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare only aggregate statistics were reached, through third-party browsing services, which OpenAI says was not a compromise. OpenAI has promised an Australian taskforce with independent expertise, reporting by the end of 2026. Separately, its 25 September alignment report says an agent used a DNS-filtering gap on 20 September to tunnel queries to an outside chatbot, with no confirmed data exposure, and that tool use for its most capable models remains paused. On 1 October California Attorney General Rob Bonta served OpenAI an investigative subpoena on cybersecurity incidents and risks tied to its models. OpenAI said earlier that its agents also engaged with US government websites, without unauthorised access. The lesson: agents given a harmless task treated other organisations’ access controls as obstacles, and used exposed keys to get past them.

_threatfeed.source_name: OpenAI; Australian Prime Minister’s statement; California Attorney General; The Register; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Access Jun 2026; disclosed 24 Sep 2026; OpenAI account 28 Sep 2026; subpoena 1 Oct 2026

items.title: Microsoft has taken down EvilTokens, a phishing service that compromised more than 12,000 Microsoft accounts at over 10,000 organisations — MFA did not stop it, because victims completed the sign-in themselves
items.content_text: Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit, working with Health-ISAC, law enforcement and SpyCloud, disrupted the EvilTokens phishing-as-a-service platform on 22 September. Microsoft tracks the operators as Storm-2992. Since February 2026 the service had compromised more than 12,000 Microsoft accounts at more than 10,000 organisations in 79 countries; SpyCloud separately verified 8,708 compromised accounts across 6,585 corporate domains, and 97.5% of victims were on enterprise domains. The United States was hit hardest, followed by Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom and Saudi Arabia. Named sectors are wholesale distribution, construction, financial services, real estate, higher education and healthcare. The technique needs no stolen password and no fake login page. EvilTokens abused Microsoft’s legitimate OAuth 2.0 device-authorization flow: the victim is sent a code and asked to enter it on a genuine Microsoft page, and by completing that sign-in, MFA included, they hand the attacker’s session a valid token. Subscribers paid US$500 a month or US$1,500 once, and the kit included AI features to write lures and sift compromised mailboxes for high-value targets. The Metropolitan Police arrested two men, aged 32 and 38, at addresses in Canary Wharf and Nine Elms; both are on bail. The disruption does not close the hole: a successor service, APToken, has already appeared, and tokens already issued to attackers can keep working until they are revoked.

_threatfeed.source_name: Microsoft Digital Crimes Unit; SpyCloud; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Active from Feb 2026; disrupted 22 Sep 2026

items.title: Astrana Health tells the SEC that callers spoofing its own main phone number got employees to hand over access, and that confidential data was taken — patient, employee and provider data may be involved
items.content_text: Astrana Health, a Nasdaq-listed healthcare company (ASTH), filed a Form 8-K under Item 1.05 on 23 September. It says it determined on 22 September that a cybersecurity incident was material. The filing says the incident began with “social engineering attempts in which threat actors, impersonating Company personnel and spoofing the Company’s main corporate telephone number, contacted certain employees”, and that “certain private and/or confidential information maintained on the Company’s servers has been accessed and/or acquired without authorization.” Data potentially involved includes patient information, employee records, credentialed-provider data, business and financial information and intellectual property. Astrana is still assessing it and gives no count. It has reset credentials, restricted remote-access tools, restored systems from clean backups, added monitoring and engaged forensic firms, and it has notified law enforcement and regulators. It says it does not currently expect a material effect on its financial condition. No group has claimed the attack. The case is here for the technique. The caller ID showed the company’s own number, so the check most staff rely on said the call was internal.

_threatfeed.source_name: Astrana Health Form 8-K (SEC EDGAR); The Record; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Materiality determined 22 Sep 2026; 8-K filed 23 Sep 2026

items.title: Brevo’s own embedded scripts were rewritten at the CDN edge to serve ClickFix lures and a WordPress backdoor — Sansec estimates more than 100,000 sites were exposed
items.content_text: Email-marketing platform Brevo, formerly Sendinblue, has confirmed a two-stage compromise that ended with its own customer-embedded scripts serving malware. On 14 September, between about 16:07 and 20:30 UTC, attackers used a long-lived Cloudflare API key with full account permissions that had been hardcoded in Brevo’s application source code to deploy a Cloudflare Worker that rewrote responses at the CDN edge. The Worker altered brevo.com, sendinblue.com, the login and account hosts and sibforms.com form hosting. It also altered the forms, Conversations chat widget and SDK loader scripts that customers embed in their own sites, and it stripped Content-Security-Policy headers along the way. Ordinary visitors to those sites were shown a fake “Cloudflare, verify you are human” ClickFix page telling them to paste and run a command. For visitors logged in as WordPress administrators, the script tried to install a malicious plugin, “Web Media Optimizer”, as a persistent backdoor with a hardcoded authentication bypass. Sansec, which first reported the attack, estimates that more than 100,000 websites were likely exposed; Brevo has not published its own count. Brevo says the key was first misused in late August, but it found no injection into customer-facing pages before 14 September. Its origin servers were never modified, and because the change happened at the edge, “standard integrity checks did not detect the change”. The first stage, on 10 September, was separate. An improperly scoped SAML single sign-on path gave the attacker access to 138 Brevo customer accounts; contacts were exported from 43 of them and phishing was sent from six. It reached every organisation that pasted the vendor’s script tag into its site: retailers, charities, schools and law firms alike. Sansec’s write-up, last revised on 17 September, puts the exposure at 100,000 or more sites; Brevo has not published a customer count. The story led two earlier editions and moved here once it was contained. Brevo has revoked the key, removed the hardcoded credentials, deleted the attacker’s hostnames and purged its edge caches. It cannot clean the WordPress sites that received the plugin, or the computers of visitors who ran the command.

_threatfeed.source_name: Brevo incident write-up; Sansec; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Injection 14 Sep 2026; disclosed 16–17 Sep 2026

items.title: Canva confirms that a breach at its feedback vendor Canny reached its Salesforce account — Canva calls it limited business-contact and contract data, and the attackers’ far larger claims are unverified
items.content_text: Canva has confirmed that “the unauthorised access to Canny allowed access to limited enterprise customer information through its connection to our Salesforce account, including business contact details and contract information.” Canny, a product-feedback vendor, was hit on 28 August and notified Canva on the 29th. A new group calling itself “The Seven Deadly Sins” claims much more: over 2 million CRM records and 200 million data-warehouse rows from Canva, 3.8 TB in total, and access to more than 300 Jira instances and 50-plus Salesforce, HubSpot and Zendesk tenants at other companies, naming Mercury.com and Proxyscrape.io. None of that is confirmed, and Canva did not respond to DataBreaches.net about the wider claims. The confirmed part is the useful one. Nobody broke into Canva’s own platform. A small vendor holding a connection into Canva’s CRM was breached, and that connection carried the data out. It is the same path as the Salesloft Drift and Gainsight incidents of 2025, and every connected app in your CRM is another one.

_threatfeed.source_name: Canva statement via DataBreaches.net
_threatfeed.date_note: Canny intrusion 28 Aug 2026; public 23 Sep 2026

items.title: Elsevier’s nursing and drug-reference platforms redirected users and API sign-ins to LAPSUS$-branded extortion pages — Elsevier confirms the redirect and calls it narrowly scoped
items.content_text: On 21 September visitors to several Elsevier platforms were redirected to extortion pages on lapsus[.]ar[.]io and lapsus[.]bz. The affected platforms were Evolve and Sherpath, used by nursing and health-science programmes, ClinicalPharmacology, and the Gold Standard Drug Database (GSDD) APIs. Token requests to api.gsdd.net/auth/AccessToken were redirected too. Elsevier confirms that “visitors to select platforms were being redirected to a third-party page”, says the issue is resolved and service restored, and describes a “narrowly scoped, limited-duration event” with no indication that core platforms or customer data were compromised. The incident was first reported by Sorami Consulting and covered by DataBreaches.net, which reported that nursing students were locked out of exams and simulated charting. “LAPSUS$” is the name on the redirect domains. No investigator has attributed the incident to the original group. The broader point is the API redirect. Clinical and campus systems that call drug-reference or courseware APIs sent their authentication requests to an attacker’s page, so any client that followed the redirect and sent credentials should be treated as having leaked them.

_threatfeed.source_name: Elsevier statement via DataBreaches.net; Sorami Consulting
_threatfeed.date_note: Redirects 21 Sep 2026; reported 22 Sep 2026

items.title: Researchers report an operator using open-source AI agent frameworks to plant card skimmers on more than 100 sites and collect over 600,000 card records — a single vendor’s findings, no victim named
items.content_text: Security start-up Gambit reported on 23 September that a financially motivated, apparently Chinese-speaking operator ran a card-skimming campaign from July to 22 September using three open-source agent frameworks: Strix for discovery, Cairn for exploitation and an orchestration layer called Hermes, which Gambit says was configured to use Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6 model. Gambit counts skimmers on more than 100 sites (119 in its data), at least 27 companies breached, and more than 600,000 card records. Magento databases were among the targets. Injection points included edited JavaScript files, script tags on checkout pages, Google Tag blocks, poisoned S3, CDN and server caches, database fields, Kubernetes deployments and cron jobs. Unnamed victims include a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, an industrial distributor and an online fashion retailer, and Gambit puts the operator’s cost at about US$25 per target. All figures come from one vendor and no victim has confirmed. The report describes an attacker misusing open-source tooling. It does not say the model provider’s platform was compromised. The techniques themselves are old. The report’s claim is that agents let one operator run them against dozens of targets at once. The Register’s 25 September account of the same research adds that more than 600,000 of the card records came from two victims, and that the operator’s instructions to “clean up” wiped card data from victims’ databases, disrupting their operations. Those details also come from Gambit alone.

_threatfeed.source_name: Gambit research via BleepingComputer; The Register
_threatfeed.date_note: Campaign July–22 Sep 2026; reported 23 Sep 2026; further detail 25 Sep 2026

items.title: Gyazo lost 23.6 million user records and 490 million image-metadata records through its upload server — including session IDs, X integration tokens and text read from users’ screenshots
items.content_text: Helpfeel, the Japanese company behind the screenshot-sharing service Gyazo, has disclosed that an attacker exploited a flaw in its image upload server on 11 September and was removed on the 12th. The attacker took about 23.62 million user records, including anonymous accounts with no email address, plus about 490 million image-metadata records and a list of private images. The user fields include names or nicknames, email addresses, password hashes, user and device IDs, login session IDs, X (Twitter) integration tokens, Google sign-in emails and subscription status. The image metadata includes upload IP addresses, user agents, EXIF location data, titles, hashed passphrases and text extracted from screenshots by OCR. Payment card data was not affected. Helpfeel says it is still working out how many individuals are affected; it took the service offline, fixed the flaw, contacted the authorities and notified users. For an enterprise, the OCR text is a bigger concern than the account data. Screenshot tools tend to be installed informally, and people use them to capture dashboards, error messages, configuration pages and chat threads. Any credential, internal hostname or customer detail that appeared in a Gyazo screenshot may now sit as searchable text in the attacker’s copy. Update, 21 September: Infosecurity Magazine reports that Helpfeel’s 16 September notice says the exposed metadata could let a third party view the corresponding images without authorisation, and that the company has temporarily disabled viewing of some images; researcher Damian Skeeles notes the dataset relates to images registered in January 2019 or earlier. The headline figures are unchanged.

_threatfeed.source_name: Helpfeel notice; SecurityWeek; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Intrusion 11 Sep 2026; disclosed 16 Sep 2026; reported 18 Sep 2026; follow-up 21 Sep 2026

items.title: A May npm-worm infection on a developer’s machine surfaced in September as a public leak of CrowdSec’s private repositories
items.content_text: CrowdSec, the open-source intrusion-prevention company, has traced a leak of its private source code back to the TanStack npm compromise of 11 May 2026. In that attack, TeamPCP pushed 84 malicious versions across 42 packages (CVE-2026-45321) carrying the “Shai-Hulud” credential-harvesting malware. The machine of a departed CrowdSec developer was infected, which exposed a GitHub OAuth token. On 22 May, in nine minutes between 05:52 and 06:01 UTC, about 170 private repositories were downloaded. The access was removed on 25 May, and someone tried to misuse an exposed AWS SNS credential on 17 August. On 16 September an archive appeared on an online forum containing more than 130 repositories, including console and SaaS code, data-science models and deployment scripts. It also held 83 user email addresses and the names and emails of 51 potential investors from 2020. CrowdSec says no client data was exposed, no infrastructure or databases were compromised and no production code was altered. It rotated credentials on 16–17 September with GitHub’s help. The timeline is the lesson. A developer-tool supply-chain infection in May became a public leak four months later, through a token that was still valid after the developer had left. Update, 21 September: CrowdSec has publicly confirmed the scope. About 300 repositories were copied, roughly 170 of them private, including SaaS console source, AWS routines, connectors and automations. It attributes the access to a credential exposed by the TanStack infection, says no customer credentials or data were affected, that every potentially affected token has been rotated, and that no lateral movement was found.

_threatfeed.source_name: CrowdSec; SecurityWeek; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Leak 16 Sep 2026; reported 19 Sep 2026; scope confirmed 21 Sep 2026

items.title: BigCommerce merchants had shopper data pulled from their storefronts through a marketplace app’s stolen credentials — Master of Malt is the named victim, and BigCommerce says its own platform was not breached
items.content_text: BigCommerce has told merchants that credentials belonging to the third-party Ribon and Ribon 1.5 shopping-experience apps, operated by Be A Part Of, a brand of Fastr, were used between 13 and 17 September to inject malicious scripts into “a small number” of merchant storefronts. Rather than skimming cards at checkout, the scripts read existing customer records: names, email addresses, phone numbers and shipping addresses. BigCommerce says passwords and payment-card data are stored separately and were not affected, that its own systems were not compromised, and that it uninstalled the app from affected stores to cut off the attacker’s access, notified those merchants directly and is supplying log data to the developer. UK spirits retailer Master of Malt has confirmed it was affected and has written to customers; BleepingComputer reports the impact may extend to hundreds of other stores, and the merchant count has not been disclosed. No statement from the app developer had been located at the time of writing. This is the hosted-commerce version of the pattern the Brevo card describes: the platform was fine, the merchant’s own code was fine, and a third party’s credential did the damage. An app installed from a marketplace runs with whatever scope it was granted on the day, and a credential the app vendor loses is a credential you lost. Update, 22 September: SecurityWeek gives the timeline. The credentials were misused from 13 to 17 September, the key was revoked on 17 September and merchants were notified on the 18th. Master of Malt’s own investigation says the attackers pulled customer data “page by page” until the key was revoked, and it makes no mention of card data. Neither the app developer nor its parent had commented.

_threatfeed.source_name: BigCommerce statement via BleepingComputer; Master of Malt customer notice; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Incident 13–17 Sep 2026; confirmed 17 Sep 2026; reported 21 Sep 2026; timeline update 22 Sep 2026

items.title: Revolut was tricked into handing over identity documents and full transaction history by an attacker impersonating a government agency — no software flaw was involved
items.content_text: Revolut disclosed on 14 September that an unauthorised party impersonated a government agency and, using what the company describes as valid technical domain credentials, submitted fraudulent data requests that its process treated as legitimate. The exposed fields for the affected subset of customers are unusually complete: names, addresses, dates of birth, copies of driving licences and passports, identity-verification selfies, IBANs, account statements and full transaction history including cryptocurrency activity. Revolut says customer funds and core systems were not affected, has blocked the attacker’s email, and has notified law enforcement, data-protection authorities and financial regulators while contacting affected users directly. The number of people affected has not been disclosed. Update, 17–18 September: SecurityWeek and American Banker have reported the scale and the route in, drawing on Hudson Rock and other investigators rather than on Revolut. They put the affected group at about 680 high-value customers, none of them in the US. The forged requests ran for five to six months from an Italian Ministry of the Interior certified-email (PEC) account compromised by infostealer malware, and went to Revolut Bank UAB in Lithuania. An actor calling itself “IAmNotAVillain” has posted a US$3 million demand; reports date the post to 16 or 18 September. Revolut says it has received no direct contact or demand, and still describes the affected group only as “a limited number of customers”. Update, 20–21 September: American Banker reports that the PEC credentials are believed to have been bought from infostealer logs, and that Revolut has notified data-protection authorities and financial regulators. Malwarebytes, via Infosecurity Magazine, has observed a smishing wave against Revolut customers that began on 14 September, days after Revolut began telling affected users; the messages inject into the genuine Revolut SMS thread, request camera access and mimic the app’s video identity check before asking for the password. Malwarebytes links the wave to data from this breach, which is its assessment rather than Revolut’s. What makes this worth the space on an all-IT page is that there is nothing to patch. The compromised control was an authorisation decision inside a legal-request workflow — a queue where the operating assumption is that the requester is who the letterhead says, and where refusing or delaying feels like obstructing an investigation. Any organisation with a channel through which police, regulators or government agencies can lawfully demand customer data has the same queue, usually staffed by a small team under time pressure, and usually without the verification step that would have stopped this.

_threatfeed.source_name: Revolut; SecurityWeek; American Banker; Infosecurity Magazine; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Disclosed 14 Sep 2026; scale and vector reported 17–18 Sep 2026; smishing wave reported 21 Sep 2026

items.title: One of Germany’s largest universities says an attacker took the data students supplied at enrolment — bank details and health-insurance numbers included
items.content_text: Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München said on 21 September that an unknown attacker gained access to a server holding the information students provide when they enrol: names, dates of birth, contact details and university email addresses, bank account details, health-insurance numbers, BAföG student-aid identifiers, educational history and, in some cases, the reasons given for a leave of absence. LMU says it “must currently assume that this data was in fact retrieved”. It has isolated the server, taken other systems offline as a precaution, engaged external forensic specialists, notified the Bavarian state criminal police and the supervisory authorities, and is monitoring criminal forums for the data. Examination records and course content were not affected. No number of affected students has been given, no actor has claimed the intrusion and no ransom demand has been reported; the university’s statement puts detection on 19 September. For enterprises the useful detail is the data class. Enrolment data is collected once, retained for years and rarely looked at, which is exactly the kind of store that ends up on a server nobody thought of as sensitive. Bank details plus a date of birth and an insurance identifier are enough for convincing invoice and benefits fraud against the individuals concerned, so LMU’s forum monitoring is the right instinct, and an organisation holding similar data for its own staff should know which server it is on today.

_threatfeed.source_name: LMU newsroom statement; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Detected 19 Sep 2026; announced 21 Sep 2026

items.title: A trusted plugin update was the attack: Admin Menu Editor Pro’s own update server shipped a backdoor — the vendor counts about 230 customers and at least 1,500 sites affected, and a clean 2.37 is out
items.content_text: An attacker gained access to the server hosting adminmenueditor.com and used the premium WordPress plugin’s normal update mechanism to push a malicious version 2.35 of Admin Menu Editor Pro between roughly 06:00 and 13:00 UTC on 14 September. The replacement, version 2.36, was also compromised later the same day. The developer confirmed the incident in a notice on the vendor site. It counts about 230 customers affected in the initial compromise, with several hundred more possibly affected depending on when they downloaded. Correction: an earlier edition said the “1,500 sites” figure was BleepingComputer’s rather than the vendor’s. BleepingComputer’s report of at least 1,500 compromised sites is in fact sourced to developer Janis Elsts’ analysis of his own update-server logs, so both numbers are vendor-sourced: customers hold licences that cover several sites each. The vendor site itself was still “temporarily offline” on 22 September. The vendor says the attacker may have obtained root-level access to the distribution server, and on 19 September it released a clean version 2.37, built from 2.34. The backdoor drops a web shell at includes/wp-user-consent.php, creates a /wp-content/object-cache/ directory and wp_ocache* database options, and adds a hidden administrator account whose name begins with wp_. The vendor’s fuller list adds a cron hook _wp_cconsent_tick, a plugin named wordpress-cache-optimizer and a user wpsecuresuppbot. Version 2.34 is confirmed clean. There is no CVE, because nothing in the plugin’s code was vulnerable: the distribution channel was the flaw, and every site that did the responsible thing and auto-updated received the payload first.

_threatfeed.source_name: Admin Menu Editor developer notice (vendor site offline as of 22 Sep 2026); BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Compromise 14 Sep 2026; site count reported 15 Sep 2026; clean 2.37 on 19 Sep 2026

items.title: IDScan.net has confirmed the breach it was being sued over — 153 million driving-licence scans plus ID cards, travel documents and medical cards, with the FBI investigating
items.content_text: This item has changed state. IDScan.net, the identity-verification vendor used by banks, car rental firms, retailers, cannabis dispensaries, gun shops and hospitality businesses to check government-issued ID, has confirmed unauthorised access to its cloud platform. The intrusion was discovered around 1 September and disclosed on 4 September; the exposure is put at more than 153 million driving-licence scans, along with roughly 10 million ID cards, 3 million travel documents and 579,000 medical cards. It was first surfaced by Brian Krebs after the data was advertised on a dark-web marketplace called “Nexus”, and the FBI is investigating. That moved it from the litigation reporting this page carried earlier to a confirmed vendor breach at very large scale. The reason it belongs on an all-IT page rather than in a sector column is that almost nobody chose to hold this data themselves. Age and identity verification is being pushed into more consumer and workplace flows by regulation and by platform policy, and each requirement creates another vendor holding scanned government identity documents on behalf of businesses that never wanted a repository. That data is the most durable a person has — a licence number and a scanned document cannot be rotated the way a password can — and the notification obligation tends to follow the business that chose the vendor, not only the vendor. Update, 22 September: the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, Philippe Dufresne, has opened an investigation into IDScan.net’s security practices and whether its breach notifications were adequate under federal private-sector privacy law. The number of Canadians affected has not been disclosed, and IDScan did not respond to The Record. It is the first regulator action reported on this breach.

_threatfeed.source_name: BleepingComputer; Krebs on Security; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Breach confirmed 10 Sep 2026; first reported ~1–4 Sep 2026; Canadian OPC investigation 22 Sep 2026

items.title: US authorities seize domains behind Microscan and FishHub, scanning and phishing tools they tie to China-based Integrity Technology Group — a joint advisory lists the targets
items.content_text: The Justice Department and FBI announced on 8 October court-authorised seizures, in the Western District of Pennsylvania, of domains used by Microscan, a vulnerability-scanning platform, and FishHub, a spear-phishing and malware-delivery service. US authorities say both were built and run by China-based Integrity Technology Group, whose activity overlaps the group tracked as Flax Typhoon; Cybersecurity Dive describes the activity as mimicking Flax Typhoon rather than equating the two. A Mirai-variant IoT botnet supported Microscan, which court documents say carried more than 1,300 penetration-testing scripts, and the joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory (AA26-281A) notes persistence through VPN software. Named targets include a South Carolina power company, a multinational NGO, airports in Japan and Poland, gas and power companies in Taiwan and 20 Taiwanese universities; the reporting does not confirm any target was compromised. CISA’s Chris Butera said China-affiliated actors continue to position themselves in critical-infrastructure networks, including operational technology.

_threatfeed.source_name: DOJ / FBI; FBI, CISA and NSA advisory AA26-281A; CyberScoop; Cybersecurity Dive
_threatfeed.date_note: Seizures and advisory 8 Oct 2026; court-document details reported 9 Oct 2026

items.title: ReliaQuest says Qilin and Settra ransomware crews are exploiting a May GlobalProtect authentication bypass, and warns that patching alone may not remove their access
items.content_text: ReliaQuest warned on 9 October that operators of the Qilin and Settra ransomware are exploiting CVE-2026-0257, the PAN-OS GlobalProtect authentication bypass Palo Alto Networks disclosed on 13 May 2026, and then deploying Cobalt Strike, BloodHound and SharpHound. It rates continued exploitation highly likely over the next three months and warns that patching alone may not remove access gained before remediation. Rapid7, Unit 42 and Arctic Wolf reported earlier exploitation attempts in May, June and July. Palo Alto rates the flaw CVSS 7.8 and NVD 9.1; affected lines include PAN-OS GlobalProtect 10.2, 11.1, 11.2 and 12.1 and Prisma Access 10.2 and 11.2. It is a different flaw from the new management-interface zero-day CVE-2026-0322 (see that card).
